Channel Partitioning.definition: **Channel Partitioning** divides a shared medium into assigned portions of time, frequency, or code.

Taking Turns.definition: **Taking Turns** coordinates shared-medium access by granting users permission in an order.

Random Access.definition: **Random Access** lets users contend for a shared medium when they have data to send.

Ethernet Frames.definition: **Ethernet Frames** carry local-link data with source and destination MAC addresses, a type field, and an error check.

MAC Addresses.definition: **MAC Addresses** identify link-layer interfaces for local frame delivery.

CSMA-CD.definition: **CSMA-CD** senses a shared Ethernet medium and detects collisions while transmitting.

Binary Exponential Backoff.definition: **Binary Exponential Backoff** increases the range of randomized retry delays after repeated collisions.

Collision Detection Window.definition: **Collision Detection Window** requires shared-Ethernet transmission time to cover the worst-case round-trip propagation delay.

Repeaters and Hubs.definition: **Repeaters and Hubs** operate at the physical layer and join segments into a shared transmission medium.

Ethernet Switching.definition: **Ethernet Switching** forwards frames between ports using destination MAC addresses.

Full-Duplex Links.definition: **Full-Duplex Links** allow simultaneous transmission in both directions on a point-to-point link.

Store-and-Forward Switching.definition: **Store-and-Forward Switching** receives a complete frame before forwarding it.

Cut-Through Switching.definition: **Cut-Through Switching** starts forwarding after enough header information arrives, before receiving the full frame.

Self-Learning Switch Tables.definition: **Self-Learning Switch Tables** learn source MAC locations from arriving frames and use them to forward destinations.

Spanning Tree Protocol.definition: **Spanning Tree Protocol** selects a loop-free active topology for bridged Ethernet.

VLANs.definition: **VLANs** divide shared switching infrastructure into separate logical layer-2 broadcast domains.

Port-Based VLANs.definition: **Port-Based VLANs** assign VLAN membership according to the switch port receiving a frame.

MAC-Based VLANs.definition: **MAC-Based VLANs** assign VLAN membership using the endpoint MAC address.

802.1Q Trunking.definition: **802.1Q Trunking** carries VLAN identity in tagged Ethernet frames across links shared by multiple VLANs.

Packet Switching.definition: **Packet Switching** shares network links by forwarding independently addressed packets as capacity becomes available.

Circuit Switching.definition: **Circuit Switching** reserves a communication path or resource allocation before data transfer.

Statistical Multiplexing.definition: **Statistical Multiplexing** shares capacity according to actual packet arrivals rather than fixed per-user slices.

Best-Effort Service.definition: **Best-Effort Service** attempts packet delivery without guaranteeing delivery, order, delay, or bandwidth.

Network Planes.definition: **Network Planes** separate packet forwarding, route computation, and administrative configuration.

Software-Defined Networking.definition: **Software-Defined Networking** places control logic in a controller that programs forwarding devices.

IPv4 Addresses.definition: **IPv4 Addresses** are 32-bit interface addresses used for network-layer delivery.

CIDR and Aggregation.definition: **CIDR and Aggregation** use arbitrary prefix lengths and combine aligned address blocks to reduce routing state.

Subnet Masks.definition: **Subnet Masks** mark which IPv4 address bits belong to the network prefix.

Network and Broadcast Addresses.definition: **Network and Broadcast Addresses** identify the all-zero and all-one host-bit endpoints of an ordinary IPv4 subnet.

Classful Addressing.definition: **Classful Addressing** is the historical fixed-size IPv4 allocation scheme with class A, B, and C unicast networks.

IPv4 Header.definition: **IPv4 Header** contains the addresses and control fields needed to carry an IPv4 datagram.

IPv4 Fragmentation.definition: **IPv4 Fragmentation** splits an oversized IPv4 datagram into smaller datagrams that fit a link MTU.

IP TTL and Traceroute.definition: **IP TTL and Traceroute** limit packet forwarding lifetime and reveal successive hops through TTL-expiry responses.

IPv4 Header Checksum.definition: **IPv4 Header Checksum** detects many errors in the IPv4 header using a one’s-complement checksum.

QoS Service Models.definition: **QoS Service Models** describe which bandwidth, loss, order, and timing properties a network service promises.

ATM Constant Bit Rate.definition: **ATM Constant Bit Rate** is the reserved constant-rate service example in the lecture’s network-service comparison.

ATM Available Bit Rate.definition: **ATM Available Bit Rate** is the lecture’s ATM example with a guaranteed minimum rate rather than a fixed constant allocation.

Integrated Services.definition: **Integrated Services** is the lecture’s Internet architecture example for explicit per-flow service guarantees.

Differentiated Services.definition: **Differentiated Services** is the lecture’s architecture example for treating classes of packets differently.

VLSM Subnetting.definition: **VLSM Subnetting** allocates differently sized aligned subnets within a larger address block.

Longest Prefix Matching.definition: **Longest Prefix Matching** chooses the matching route with the most specific destination prefix.

Router Architecture.definition: **Router Architecture** separates input processing, a switching fabric, output processing, and routing control.

Memory Switching.definition: **Memory Switching** moves packets between router ports by copying through shared memory.

Bus Switching.definition: **Bus Switching** transfers packets across a shared internal bus from input to output memory.

Crossbar and Clos Switching.definition: **Crossbar and Clos Switching** use interconnected switching elements to support parallel internal packet transfers.

Input Queuing and HOL Blocking.definition: **Input Queuing and HOL Blocking** hold packets before the fabric, where a blocked first packet can delay packets behind it.

Output Queuing and Scheduling.definition: **Output Queuing and Scheduling** buffer packets awaiting an output link and choose the next packet to transmit.

Patricia Tries.definition: **Patricia Tries** organize address prefixes in a compressed bitwise search tree for forwarding lookup.

TCAM.definition: **TCAM** matches keys in parallel against stored bit patterns containing zero, one, and don’t-care values.

Generalized Forwarding.definition: **Generalized Forwarding** matches selected packet-header fields and applies a configured action.

Content-Addressable Memory.definition: **Content-Addressable Memory** retrieves entries by matching stored content rather than supplying an ordinary memory location.

Names Addresses and Indirection.definition: **Names Addresses and Indirection** separate human-readable identity, topological location, and local interface delivery.

Soft State.definition: **Soft State** expires unless refreshed, allowing stale information to disappear without explicit cleanup.

DHCP.definition: **DHCP** automatically supplies an interface with an IP configuration and a lease.

DHCP Leases and Reservations.definition: **DHCP Leases and Reservations** control how long an allocation lasts and whether an endpoint receives a configured fixed assignment.

ARP.definition: **ARP** resolves an on-link IPv4 next-hop address to a link-layer address.

DNS Hierarchy and Zones.definition: **DNS Hierarchy and Zones** distribute name records through delegated authority rather than one flat global file.

Recursive DNS Queries.definition: **Recursive DNS Queries** ask a DNS server to obtain an answer on the requester’s behalf.

Iterative DNS Queries.definition: **Iterative DNS Queries** ask for an answer or a referral, leaving the requester to contact the next server.

DNS Caching.definition: **DNS Caching** reuses DNS results until their allowed cache lifetime expires.

Negative DNS Caching.definition: **Negative DNS Caching** temporarily remembers DNS nonexistence or missing-record results.

DNS Resource Records.definition: **DNS Resource Records** store typed name-to-value information with a cache lifetime.

DNS A Records.definition: **DNS A Records** map a DNS name to an IPv4 address.

DNS NS Records.definition: **DNS NS Records** identify the DNS servers authoritative for a domain or delegated zone.

DNS CNAME Records.definition: **DNS CNAME Records** map an alias name to another canonical DNS name.

DNS MX Records.definition: **DNS MX Records** identify mail exchanger hostnames and their delivery preferences for a domain.

DNS Reliability.definition: **DNS Reliability** combines replicated servers, retries, timeouts, and response matching to survive failures.

Shortest-Path Routing.definition: **Shortest-Path Routing** chooses paths minimizing a common sum of link costs.

Link-State Routing.definition: **Link-State Routing** floods link information so each router can compute routes from a network graph.

Dijkstra Algorithm.definition: **Dijkstra Algorithm** computes shortest paths by repeatedly finalizing the smallest tentative distance.

Distance-Vector Routing.definition: **Distance-Vector Routing** learns destination distances from neighbors rather than distributing the whole topology.

Bellman-Ford Updates.definition: **Bellman-Ford Updates** compute a node’s distance as the minimum link-plus-neighbor advertised distance.

Path-Vector Routing.definition: **Path-Vector Routing** advertises a destination path so nodes can reject loops and apply path policies.

OSPF.definition: **OSPF** is a link-state interior routing protocol used to compute paths within an autonomous system.

IS-IS.definition: **IS-IS** is a link-state interior routing protocol named alongside OSPF in the lectures.

RIP.definition: **RIP** is a distance-vector interior routing protocol with hop-count metrics and bounded infinity.

EIGRP.definition: **EIGRP** is an advanced distance-vector routing protocol named as a distance-vector example in the deck.

MPLS Label Switching.definition: **MPLS Label Switching** forwards encapsulated packets using labels that identify a forwarding path or class.

RSVP Signaling.definition: **RSVP Signaling** establishes path-related state through messages exchanged before the associated data forwarding.

Failure Detection.definition: **Failure Detection** infers link or neighbor failure from local signals or missing liveness messages.

Routing Convergence.definition: **Routing Convergence** is the transition toward consistent routing and forwarding after a change.

Forwarding Blackholes.definition: **Forwarding Blackholes** discard or strand traffic along a route that cannot complete delivery.

Transient Forwarding Loops.definition: **Transient Forwarding Loops** arise when routers temporarily use incompatible forwarding decisions during updates.

Count to Infinity.definition: **Count to Infinity** is slow distance-vector failure propagation caused by neighbors repeatedly trusting stale distances.

Poison Reverse.definition: **Poison Reverse** advertises a route as unreachable to the neighbor currently used to reach that destination.

BGP Session Liveness.definition: **BGP Session Liveness** uses keepalives and a hold timer to detect a silent BGP peer.

BGP Path Exploration.definition: **BGP Path Exploration** tries successive alternate paths while withdrawals and changed routes propagate.

Stable Paths Problem.definition: **Stable Paths Problem** models routing as permitted paths and local rankings that must be mutually consistent.

Policy Oscillation.definition: **Policy Oscillation** is repeated route change caused by incompatible preferences rather than a new physical failure each time.

Autonomous Systems.definition: **Autonomous Systems** are networks under a common routing administration represented by AS numbers.

BGP.definition: **BGP** exchanges prefix reachability and policy attributes between routing peers.

AS Path.definition: **AS Path** lists the AS sequence associated with a BGP route advertisement.

BGP Next-Hop Resolution.definition: **BGP Next-Hop Resolution** combines an external-prefix route with an internal route to its BGP next-hop address.

BGP Import Policy.definition: **BGP Import Policy** filters or changes received routes before local route selection.

BGP Export Policy.definition: **BGP Export Policy** controls which selected routes are advertised to each neighbor and with which attributes.

Local Preference.definition: **Local Preference** ranks BGP routes within an AS, with higher values preferred.

AS Path Prepending.definition: **AS Path Prepending** adds repeated copies of an AS number to make an advertised path look longer.

eBGP.definition: **eBGP** exchanges BGP routes between peers in different autonomous systems.

iBGP.definition: **iBGP** distributes BGP reachability and policy information among routers within one AS.

Hot-Potato Routing.definition: **Hot-Potato Routing** chooses the nearest eligible exit to hand traffic to another network quickly.

Customer-Provider Relationships.definition: **Customer-Provider Relationships** exchange payment for transit and impose directional route-export expectations.

Peering.definition: **Peering** exchanges traffic between two networks and their customers without offering unrestricted transit.

Gao-Rexford Conditions.definition: **Gao-Rexford Conditions** are commercial-policy constraints sufficient for stable interdomain routing under the model’s assumptions.

Valley-Free Paths.definition: **Valley-Free Paths** follow zero or more customer-to-provider edges, at most one peer edge, then provider-to-customer edges.

Default Routes.definition: **Default Routes** provide a fallback next hop for destinations lacking a more specific matching route.

IP Anycast.definition: **IP Anycast** routes a shared service address toward one of several announcing instances.

IP Multicast.definition: **IP Multicast** delivers a packet to interested members of a group using replication within the network.

Multicast Group Addresses.definition: **Multicast Group Addresses** identify IPv4 destination groups in 224.0.0.0/4 rather than individual source interfaces.

Iterated Unicast.definition: **Iterated Unicast** sends a separate unicast copy of the same data to every intended receiver.

Overlay Multicast.definition: **Overlay Multicast** builds application-level distribution paths on top of ordinary unicast delivery.

Shared Multicast Trees.definition: **Shared Multicast Trees** use one group distribution structure shared by multiple sources.

Source-Based Multicast Trees.definition: **Source-Based Multicast Trees** root distribution paths at a particular sender.

Minimum Spanning Trees.definition: **Minimum Spanning Trees** connect all vertices of a weighted graph with minimum total edge cost and no cycles.

Prim Algorithm.definition: **Prim Algorithm** grows a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge crossing its current cut.

Kruskal Algorithm.definition: **Kruskal Algorithm** builds a minimum spanning tree by adding cheapest edges that do not create a cycle.

IGMPv1.definition: **IGMPv1** reports IPv4 multicast group interest between hosts and their local multicast router.

IGMPv2.definition: **IGMPv2** adds explicit leave behavior, group-specific queries, and querier election to local multicast membership.

IGMPv3.definition: **IGMPv3** expresses multicast membership with source inclusion or exclusion filters.

IGMP Snooping.definition: **IGMP Snooping** lets a layer-2 switch observe membership messages to limit multicast forwarding to interested ports.

Core-Based Trees.definition: **Core-Based Trees** join multicast receivers to a distribution tree organized around designated core routers.

Reverse Path Forwarding.definition: **Reverse Path Forwarding** accepts multicast data on the interface expected to lead back toward its source.

Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting.definition: **Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting** stops reverse-path broadcast at leaf networks without interested group members.

Reverse Path Multicasting.definition: **Reverse Path Multicasting** prunes reverse-path distribution branches that have no downstream group interest.

PIM Dense Mode.definition: **PIM Dense Mode** assumes broad multicast interest and forwards unless branches have been pruned.

PIM Sparse Mode.definition: **PIM Sparse Mode** builds multicast distribution through explicit joins, initially using a rendezvous-point shared tree.

PIM Rendezvous Point.definition: **PIM Rendezvous Point** is the group meeting point that anchors PIM-SM’s initial shared tree.

PIM Register.definition: **PIM Register** encapsulates a source’s initial multicast data for unicast delivery from its DR to the RP.

PIM SPT Switchover.definition: **PIM SPT Switchover** moves receiver delivery from the RP shared tree toward a source-rooted shortest-path tree.

Wireless Network Types.definition: **Wireless Network Types** classify infrastructure use and hop count separately from whether hosts move.

Path Loss.definition: **Path Loss** reduces received signal strength as radio propagation and obstacles attenuate a transmission.

Radio Interference.definition: **Radio Interference** adds competing electromagnetic energy that can impair reception.

Multipath Propagation.definition: **Multipath Propagation** delivers delayed reflected copies of a radio signal to a receiver.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio and BER.definition: **Signal-to-Noise Ratio and BER** relate received signal quality to the probability of bit errors for a chosen physical-layer scheme.

Rate Adaptation.definition: **Rate Adaptation** changes the physical transmission rate or modulation as channel conditions vary.

CDMA.definition: **CDMA** separates simultaneous transmissions using distinct spreading codes.

Wireless Channels.definition: **Wireless Channels** divide radio spectrum into selectable frequency resources for communication.

Wi-Fi Association.definition: **Wi-Fi Association** attaches a station to an access point for participation in its wireless service set.

Passive Scanning.definition: **Passive Scanning** discovers access points by listening for their beacon transmissions.

Active Scanning.definition: **Active Scanning** discovers access points by sending probe requests and collecting probe responses.

CSMA-CA.definition: **CSMA-CA** uses sensing, randomized waiting, and acknowledgments to reduce wireless collisions.

Hidden Terminals.definition: **Hidden Terminals** cannot hear each other but can interfere at a common receiver.

Exposed Terminals.definition: **Exposed Terminals** defer because of sensed activity even when their own transmission could be noninterfering.

RTS and CTS.definition: **RTS and CTS** reserve a wireless exchange through a short request and receiver response before data.

Network Allocation Vector.definition: **Network Allocation Vector** tracks a wireless reservation duration for virtual carrier sensing.

Wi-Fi Frame Addressing.definition: **Wi-Fi Frame Addressing** distinguishes immediate radio receiver/transmitter from original frame source/destination.

Same-Subnet Roaming.definition: **Same-Subnet Roaming** changes a station’s access point while retaining its IP subnet and potentially its IP address.

Wireless Power Management.definition: **Wireless Power Management** saves energy by coordinating sleep intervals with buffered delivery and periodic wakeups.

Bluetooth Piconets.definition: **Bluetooth Piconets** coordinate nearby devices through a controller and shared time/frequency hopping resources.

Wireless Error Recovery.definition: **Wireless Error Recovery** uses local coding, detection, retries, or rate changes to handle an error-prone radio hop.

2G Circuit-Switched Core.definition: **2G Circuit-Switched Core** organizes the lecture’s legacy voice network around base stations, controllers, and mobile switching centers.

3G Parallel Voice and Data.definition: **3G Parallel Voice and Data** adds a packet-data core alongside the existing circuit-oriented voice core in the lecture model.

LTE All-IP Core.definition: **LTE All-IP Core** carries cellular service traffic through an IP packet core with separate mobility control functions.

UE and Subscriber Identity.definition: **UE and Subscriber Identity** distinguish the mobile device and subscription identity from its current network-layer location.

LTE eNodeB.definition: **LTE eNodeB** is the LTE radio base station that manages cells and connects user traffic to the packet core.

LTE Home Subscriber Server.definition: **LTE Home Subscriber Server** stores home-subscriber information used in authentication and mobility management.

LTE Mobility Management Entity.definition: **LTE Mobility Management Entity** coordinates subscriber authentication, mobility state, paging, and tunnel setup in the control plane.

LTE Serving Gateway.definition: **LTE Serving Gateway** forwards user traffic between radio-access tunnel endpoints and the packet gateway.

LTE Packet Gateway.definition: **LTE Packet Gateway** connects the cellular packet core to external packet networks such as the Internet.

LTE PDCP.definition: **LTE PDCP** provides packet-data convergence functions such as header compression and encryption at the radio edge.

LTE RLC.definition: **LTE RLC** handles radio-link fragmentation/reassembly and reliable transfer functions in the lecture stack.

LTE Radio Scheduling.definition: **LTE Radio Scheduling** allocates radio time-frequency opportunities to active user equipment.

OFDM.definition: **OFDM** multiplexes data over orthogonal frequency subcarriers.

GTP Tunnels.definition: **GTP Tunnels** encapsulate user packets across cellular core segments while access locations change.

LTE Attachment and System Information.definition: **LTE Attachment and System Information** discovers a base station and establishes the control and data state needed for cellular service.

LTE Sleep and Paging.definition: **LTE Sleep and Paging** reduce radio energy use while maintaining enough location knowledge to reach a mobile when needed.

5G New Radio.definition: **5G New Radio** extends the cellular radio system using new spectrum and antenna techniques aimed at greater capacity and lower delay.

MIMO.definition: **MIMO** uses multiple antennas to provide spatial transmission or reception capabilities.

Mobile Identity and Location.definition: **Mobile Identity and Location** separate a persistent endpoint or subscriber identity from its current point of attachment.

Home and Visited Networks.definition: **Home and Visited Networks** distinguish the subscriber’s registered provider from the network currently providing access.

Mobile IP Registration.definition: **Mobile IP Registration** binds a mobile’s home address to its current care-of locator for redirected delivery.

IP Tunneling.definition: **IP Tunneling** carries an original packet inside an outer packet addressed to a tunnel endpoint.

Indirect Mobile Routing.definition: **Indirect Mobile Routing** delivers traffic through a home-side anchor that forwards it to the mobile’s current location.

Triangle Routing.definition: **Triangle Routing** is the detour through a mobile’s home anchor when a more direct correspondent-to-mobile path exists.

Direct Mobile Routing.definition: **Direct Mobile Routing** uses the mobile’s current locator to deliver without the home-anchor data-path detour.

Cellular Handover.definition: **Cellular Handover** moves an active mobile to another base station while updating radio and tunnel state.

Wireless Effects on Transport.definition: **Wireless Effects on Transport** change loss and delay behavior even though the underlying IP service remains best effort.
